solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Possible lead in to making a phone call?

definitions.text: Possible lead in to making a phone call?

blocks.clueFragment: Possible lead in to making a phone call?
blocks.note: surface reading: an opening line or excuse someone might use to start a conversation by phone
setter's reading: the literal sound heard on the line just before you begin dialling

explanation.surface: Someone hunting for a pretext or opening line before ringing somebody up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead in' suggests an opening remark or excuse for calling; read literally, it is whatever comes first, before any number is pressed.
explanation.definitionFit: The steady hum a handset emits signals the line is ready, so it literally precedes every outgoing call.

clue.text: Unambiguous order

blocks.note: first meaning: straightforward, plain-spoken, adjective
second meaning: to instruct or command, verb

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read like an adjective and noun, a clear instruction, but each is a separate meaning of one word, the second taken as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank speech is plain and straightforward; to command someone is to tell them what they must do.

clue.text: Country inn, a great resort

indicators.note: to re-sort is to sort again, putting these letters into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rural pub described as a splendid holiday destination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' looks like a holiday place, but read as re-sort it is the signal to rearrange; 'Country' is the definition, not part of 'country inn'.
explanation.definitionFit: Argentina is a nation in South America, so it is an example of a sovereign state.

clue.text: Tudors in Tunics — a new play by the Bard

indicators.note: something new has been remade, so these letters come out in a different arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fresh Shakespeare production staged with Tudor characters dressed in tunics.
explanation.walkthrough: The fifteen letters of 'Tudors in Tunics' plus 'a' rearrange into the whole title; the Bard is the usual nickname for Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Titus Andronicus is Shakespeare's early Roman revenge tragedy, so it is one of his dramatic works.

clue.text: New North Surrey garden centre

indicators.note: something made new is reworked, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: N is the compass abbreviation for north
taken as written

explanation.surface: A newly opened garden centre in the northern part of Surrey.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is an English county just south-west of London; here it is simply letters to rearrange along with N.
explanation.definitionFit: A nursery is a place where plants are raised and sold, which is what a garden centre does.

clue.text: The state of Sarkozy’s wife out East

indicators.note: read as outside, these letters sit on the outside of another piece

blocks.note: Carla Bruni, singer and model, married the French president Nicolas Sarkozy
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Wondering what condition the French first lady is in while travelling in the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' reads as a condition, but it is a country; 'out East' looks like a location yet is the instruction to put Bruni outside E.
explanation.definitionFit: Brunei is a small sultanate on Borneo, so it is an independent nation or sovereign country.

clue.text: Lift drapes when Austrian heretic is murdered

indicators.note: something murdered is destroyed and mangled, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Opening the curtains at the moment a heretic from Austria is killed, like a grim stage drama.
explanation.walkthrough: The fifteen letters of the two words rearrange exactly into the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Drapes are curtains, and to lift them is the literal action of starting a theatrical performance.

clue.text: Determined to reject memos

indicators.note: rejecting something sends it back, so in a down clue the letters are turned around

blocks.note: set on, as in being set on doing something, means determined

explanation.surface: Someone resolved to refuse the office memoranda sent their way.
explanation.walkthrough: The two-word phrase 'set on' supplies the letters; read backwards it spells NOTES.
explanation.definitionFit: Brief written messages passed around an office are memoranda, a common synonym for short jotted messages.

clue.text: Where striker stands for more pay?

blocks.note: first meaning, read as two words: in the crease, where the batter on strike stands in cricket
second meaning: a rise in wages

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a worker on strike standing on a picket line for a rise; in cricket the striker is the batter facing the bowling, who stands in the crease, the marked line at the wicket.
explanation.definitionFit: A pay rise is a boost in salary, so more pay is an upward change in earnings.

clue.text: Roman ruler will grab girl, we’re told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the letters come from a sound

blocks.note: to grab is to seize, and the girl is her

explanation.surface: Gossip that the Roman emperor is going to carry off a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: In British pronunciation the title and the phrase 'seize her' sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar was the title of Roman emperors, after Julius Caesar, so it names a ruler of Rome.

clue.text: Spot on brilliant book overlooked

indicators.note: something overlooked is missed out, so that piece is left out

blocks.note: bright and brilliant both mean shining or clever
B is a standard abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: A splendid book that has been unfairly ignored, with the critic exactly right about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Take B away from BRIGHT; 'Spot on' looks like part of the picture but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Spot on is an informal British phrase for exactly correct, which is a synonym for the answer.

clue.text: Forged article is true to life

indicators.note: something forged is hammered into shape or faked, so these letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A counterfeit item so convincing it looks just like the genuine thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forged' seems to describe the article, but it is the signal to rearrange 'article is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lifelike convincingly represents things as they actually are, which is the sense of the adjective.

clue.text: Tins of wine special constable imbibed, upset

indicators.note: to imbibe is to drink in, so one piece takes another inside it
upset means turned over, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: SC is the abbreviation for a special constable, a volunteer police officer in Britain
retsina is a Greek resin-flavoured wine

explanation.surface: A volunteer policeman drank tins of wine and got upset.
explanation.walkthrough: The container is built first and only then reversed as a whole; a special constable is a part-time volunteer police officer in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Canisters are metal containers with lids, the same thing as tins for storing food or drink.

clue.text: For starters, even nowadays, Surrey usually enforce follow on

indicators.note: starters are the opening parts, so only the leading letter of each word counts

blocks.note: the initial letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: A cricket remark: Surrey still tend to make opponents bat again when they can.
explanation.walkthrough: To enforce the follow-on in cricket is to make the side batting second bat again straight away; 'follow on' doubles as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensue is to happen afterwards as a result, the same as coming next or following.

clue.text: Youngster recalled desire for offal

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the letters are brought back in the opposite order

blocks.note: a kid is a child
a yen is a longing

explanation.surface: A child remembering a craving for organ meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalled' looks like memory, but here it means called back, turning the second piece round; 'for' simply links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Offal is the edible internal organs of an animal, and a kidney is one example of such meat.

clue.text: Puts back in the oven — but there’s a difficulty

indicators.note: a difficulty is trouble, and letters in trouble are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Warming leftovers again, only to find there is a problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'there's a' reads as ordinary grammar, but its seven letters are the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To warm cooked food again by returning it to an oven is exactly what the verb describes.

clue.text: Scientific instrument bathed city in a flickering light

indicators.note: to bathe something is to surround it completely, so one piece wraps another
being within something means sitting inside it, so these letters go inside

blocks.note: a strobe is a light that flashes rapidly
LA is Los Angeles

explanation.surface: A device that lit up a whole city with flashing light.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scientific instrument' looks like the subject of 'bathed', but it is the definition; the city sits inside the flashing light, which keeps its 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: An astrolabe is an old astronomical device for measuring the altitude of stars, used in navigation.

clue.text: Lass strode along and moved fast

blocks.note: a gal is a girl
to lope is to run with long easy strides

explanation.surface: A young woman walked briskly and then broke into a run.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes all three verbs one person's actions; the first two words build the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To gallop is to run at full speed, like a horse at its quickest gait, so it means went rapidly.

clue.text: Could be danger from garden, for example

definitions.text: Could be danger from garden, for example

blocks.note: surface reading: some hazard lurking in the garden, such as a poisonous plant
setter's reading: the six letters of one word rearrange into the other, an instance of a wordplay device

explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a warning about a hazard in the garden; actually the letters of 'garden' reshuffle into 'danger', and the answer names that kind of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A word formed by rearranging another's letters is this device, and these two words illustrate it exactly.

clue.text: Claim a point out of spite

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or disordered, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
a point of the compass, here east

explanation.surface: Someone scoring a point purely out of vindictiveness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of spite' is a set phrase, but 'out' is the anagram signal and 'of' merely links; a point in crosswords is often a compass letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Malice is the wish to harm others, the same ill will that drives spiteful behaviour.

clue.text: Company back in former position

indicators.note: going back means running in the other direction, so the letters are turned round
being in something means sitting inside it, so these letters go within another word

blocks.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
late means former, as in the late chairman

explanation.surface: A firm returning to the post it used to hold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Position' is a verb here, not the noun the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To position something is to put it in a particular place, which is one meaning of the verb to locate.

clue.text: Young form-filler

blocks.note: surface reading: a youngster completing a paper questionnaire
setter's reading: a form is the shallow hollow where a hare lies, so its occupant is a hare, here a young one

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a child filling in paperwork; a form is also the nest-like resting place of a hare.
explanation.definitionFit: A leveret is a hare in its first year, and hares rest in hollows called forms.

clue.text: Speedy, small companies’ cars

blocks.note: fleet means swift
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: Little firms that run fast vehicles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet' as an adjective for quick-moving is old-fashioned but standard.
explanation.definitionFit: Firms that own many vehicles for staff call the whole group their fleet, so several firms have fleets.

clue.text: Carol rejected consuming bit of microwaved fruit

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters run the other way
to consume is to take in, so one piece swallows another
a bit is only a small part, so just the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: a noel is a Christmas carol
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Carol turns down a piece of fruit that has been through the microwave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carol' reads as a woman's name, but it is a Christmas song; the reversed word takes in the letter M.
explanation.definitionFit: A lemon is a sour yellow citrus, an everyday example of a fruit.

clue.text: Middle-distance runner turning up from the preliminaries

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning upward means reading from bottom to top
taken from within a longer word, so the letters lie inside it

blocks.note: the run of letters sitting just after the first P

explanation.surface: An athlete emerging from the heats to reach the final.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning up' looks like arriving, but it reverses the letters found inside 'preliminaries'.
explanation.definitionFit: A miler races over one mile, which falls in athletics' middle-distance category between sprints and long distance.

clue.text: City supply of organs

blocks.note: a liver is an organ of the body
a pool is a shared stock or supply, as in a car pool

explanation.surface: A city's stock of transplant organs, or of church organs.
explanation.walkthrough: A pool of livers, read in reverse order: the supply comes second in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Liverpool is a major port in north-west England, so it is an example of a large urban centre.

clue.text: In which real cop in charge crashed?

definitions.text: In which real cop in charge crashed?

indicators.note: something crashed is smashed and scattered, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
IC is the abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A genuine officer at the wheel had an accident in which vehicle?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines: the vehicle an actual officer was driving when it crashed, while its words also supply the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A patrol vehicle is what a serving officer drives on duty, so it is where such a crash would happen.

clue.text: A vigil alert

blocks.note: taken as written
a watch kept over a dead body before burial

explanation.surface: Someone keeping watch through the night and staying watchful.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface links vigils with staying up, which disguises that 'vigil' supplies WAKE.
explanation.definitionFit: Being alert means not asleep and fully conscious, which is the adjective's meaning.

clue.text: I’d flipped over, repose being most terrible

indicators.note: flipping something over turns it the other way round

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
repose is rest

explanation.surface: Someone tossing and turning in bed, their sleep at its worst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipped over' suggests turning in bed but reverses ID.
explanation.definitionFit: Dire means dreadful, so its superlative describes the worst or most dreadful of all.

clue.text: Sweet comment about shambles

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a note is a brief remark
a shambles is a mess

explanation.surface: A kind remark about a chaotic situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' looks like an adjective describing the comment, but it is the British word for a dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton mess is an English pudding of crushed meringue, strawberries and cream, so it is a dessert.
